answer_text:
# 🦴 Bones of the Head

The human skull is generally considered to consist of **22 bones** — **8 cranial bones** and **14 facial skeleton bones**. Some sources also include the hyoid bone or the three ossicles of the middle ear (malleus, incus, and stapes), bringing the total to 29.

The skull is divided into two regions: the **neurocranium** (which protects the brain) and the **viscerocranium** (which forms the face).

---

## 🧠 Part 1: The Cranial Bones (Neurocranium) — 8 Bones

The cranium is composed of eight bones known as the cranial bones: the **frontal bone**, a **parietal bone** on each side, a **temporal bone** on each side, the **occipital bone**, the **ethmoid bone**, and the **sphenoid bone**.

Here's a breakdown of each:

| Bone | Description |
|------|-------------|
| **Frontal Bone** (×1) | A single, seamless bone that gives the forehead its structure. |
| **Parietal Bones** (×2) | Form the sides and uppermost portion of the dome of the cranium. |
| **Temporal Bones** (×2) | Form the lower lateral sides of the skull. They subdivide into petrous, squamous, zygomatic, and mastoid parts; the petrous portion houses the inner ear. |
| **Occipital Bone** (×1) | Forms the base of the cranium and has a central opening (foramen magnum) to admit the spinal cord. |
| **Sphenoid Bone** (×1) | A single bone below and in front of the brain, but behind the bones making up the face. It also forms part of the lower rear of the eye sockets. |
| **Ethmoid Bone** (×1) | Forms part of the cranial floor. |

---

## 😊 Part 2: The Facial Bones (Viscerocranium) — 14 Bones

The facial skeleton supports the soft tissues of the face and consists of 14 bones, which fuse to house the orbits of the eyes, the nasal and oral cavities, and the sinuses.

The 14 bones of the facial skeleton are: the **vomer**, two **inferior nasal conchae**, two **nasal bones**, two **maxilla**, the **mandible**, two **palatine bones**, two **zygomatic bones**, and two **lacrimal bones**.

| Bone | Description |
|------|-------------|
| **Mandible** (×1) | Makes up the lower jaw and is the **only bone of the skull that moves**. |
| **Maxilla** (×2) | One on the left and one on the right, they form the top jaw and anchor the upper teeth. |
| **Zygomatic Bones** (×2) | The cheekbones, which join with the temporal and maxillary bones to form the zygomatic arch below the eye socket. |
| **Nasal Bones** (×2) | Small bones that form the bridge of the nose. |
| **Palatine Bones** (×2) | Form the roof of the mouth and help to form the mouth cavity. |
| **Lacrimal Bones** (×2) | Small bones located in the inner wall of each eye socket (orbit). |
| **Inferior Nasal Conchae** (×2) | Help form the nasal cavity along with the vomer and nasal bones. |
| **Vomer** (×1) | A thin, flat bone forming the lower part of the nasal septum. |

---

## 🔗 How Are the Bones Connected?

Sutures are a type of fibrous joint unique to the skull. They are immovable and fuse completely around the age of 20. The three main sutures are:

- **Coronal suture** — fuses the frontal bone with the two parietal bones.
- **Sagittal suture** — fuses both parietal bones to each other.
- **Lambdoid suture** — fuses the occipital bone to the two parietal bones.

The **only synovial (movable) joint** in the skull is the **temporomandibular joint (TMJ)**, a movable connection between the mandible and the temporal bone.

---

> 💡 **Fun Fact:** The skull is embryologically derived from mesoderm and neural crest, and will fuse, harden, and mold from gestation through adulthood. It gives the human face its form, and even minor variations in anatomy among individuals can lead to vast differences in appearance.
